posts.week: FIBA World Cup · Group play report card
posts.imageAlt: We Know the W Team USA impact report card featuring official WNBA headshots and group play ratings
posts.storyImageCaption: The W Impact Score blends 60 percent official FIBA production with 40 percent role execution, lineup control, defense and game context.
posts.dek: Three wins do not mean twelve identical performances. Breanna Stewart sets the standard, Chelsea Gray and Aliyah Boston receive credit the box score misses, and Caitlin Clark’s passing cannot completely erase 30.4 percent shooting.

rows: USA’s two way anchor leads the team at 18.0 efficiency and 8.3 rebounds per game.
Efficient connecting play, 10.3 points, 3.7 assists and 2.6 steals plus blocks per game.
A team high 11.3 points on 53.8 percent shooting, plus the calmest closing possessions.
Interior activity produced 8.7 points, 6.0 rebounds and 2.3 steals plus blocks per game.
Seven rebounds and 2.0 steals plus blocks per game created major value in a two game sample.
A team high 1.7 steals and a plus 16.0 average margin reflect point of attack pressure.
Interior gravity, screening and a plus 14.7 average margin create value beyond her scoring line.
Pace control and lineup organization matter more than her modest scoring total suggests.
Switching value and rebounding helped, but her offensive influence was quieter than expected.
Her team high 6.3 assists lift the offense, but 30.4 percent shooting caps the grade.
Rebounding helped, but 21.4 percent shooting left too much offensive value on the table.
The 54.5 percent shooting was clean, but a 10.5 minute role cannot outrank larger two way responsibilities.

sections.title: The grade measures impact, not just the box score
paragraphs: Team USA finished group play 3 and 0, but a report card should explain how the wins were built, not hand everyone the same gold star. The W Impact Score gives 60 percent of the grade to official FIBA production and 40 percent to role execution, lineup control, defensive responsibility and game context.

That distinction matters. A reserve can shoot efficiently in a narrow assignment without carrying the same burden as a starter who organizes possessions, anchors coverages or absorbs the opponent’s best matchup. This is a three game Team USA snapshot, not a career ranking.

sections.title: Stewart sets the curve, Young owns the closer minutes
paragraphs: Breanna Stewart earns the top grade because she has been USA’s most complete player. Her 18.0 efficiency rating leads the team, her 8.3 rebounds stabilize the interior and her decisions connect both ends of the floor. Paige Bueckers follows with efficient offense, 3.7 assists and 2.6 combined steals and blocks per game.

Jackie Young completes the A tier. She leads USA at 11.3 points per game, is shooting 53.8 percent and delivered the late control that kept Italy from finishing its upset bid. When a game tightened, Young did not blink.

sections.title: Reese, Iriafen and Howard built the pressure layer
paragraphs: Angel Reese has supplied the most consistent interior disruption outside Stewart. Her rebounding, hands and physicality translate whether she scores or not. Kiki Iriafen made a similar impact in only two appearances, while Rhyne Howard gave USA the point of attack defense and deflections needed to speed opponents up.
Their grades reward repeatable tournament skills. Rebounding travels. Ball pressure travels. Defensive possessions that end without a second chance travel.

sections.title: Why Boston and Gray grade above Citron
paragraphs: Aliyah Boston and Chelsea Gray are the clearest examples of why this cannot be a raw efficiency ranking. Boston’s screens, interior positioning and plus 14.7 average margin shape possessions before the box score records anything. Gray organizes spacing, controls tempo and places teammates where their strengths matter.

Sonia Citron has been efficient in her 10.5 minutes per game, but the role is smaller and the responsibility is lighter. Clean execution deserves credit. It does not automatically outweigh the burden carried by Boston and Gray.

sections.title: Clark’s passing keeps her afloat, her shooting pulls her down
paragraphs: Caitlin Clark leads USA with 6.3 assists per game and owns the team’s best average plus minus. Those are real impact markers. So is 30.4 percent shooting, including 25 percent from three.

A 74 is not a dismissal of her playmaking. It reflects the full job. Clark has created quality offense for others, but the missed shots have kept her individual impact below the players delivering on both efficiency and role.

sections.title: What carries into the knockout rounds
paragraphs: USA’s 88.7 team composite score reflects a strong unbeaten start with room to sharpen. The safest formula is Stewart as the two way hub, Young as the pressure release, Bueckers as the connector and the Reese, Iriafen, Howard group keeping the defense active.

The ceiling rises if Clark’s shot normalizes and Gray’s command begins producing cleaner half court offense. Team USA already has enough talent to win. The report card asks which players are making that talent function.

debates: Should lineup control count as heavily as scoring efficiency when grading a tournament team?
How high can Clark’s grade climb if her shooting catches up to her passing in the knockout rounds?

foodSegment.title: Shak’s bite: winning earns respect, not automatic A’s
foodSegment.script: A 3 and 0 record tells us Team USA handled the assignment. It does not tell us every player handled the same assignment. Stewart has been the standard, Young has been the closer, and the next jump depends on turning Clark’s creation and Gray’s control into cleaner half court possessions.

posts.title: One Possession From Overtime: How Two Near Upsets Almost Rewrote the World Cup
posts.imageAlt: Trinity San Antonio walking toward the court in her Puerto Rico uniform at the 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup
posts.dek: Puerto Rico and Italy lost by five combined points. One more make might have changed the bracket, while Trinity San Antonio left behind the tournament's loudest defensive case.

sections.title: Five points from a different bracket
paragraphs: Puerto Rico came within three points of China, while Italy came within two of Australia. Overtime was one clean possession away in both games, but the losses were built before the final shot. China made 57.1 percent of its twos and closed a 66 to 66 game with the decisive run. Italy erased most of a 26 point deficit, yet spent too much energy repairing three quarters of damage.

That makes the what if worth considering. Puerto Rico had the best individual force on the floor in Trinity San Antonio. Italy had all the momentum after a 31 to 13 fourth quarter. Extra time guarantees neither upset, but it could have changed the emotional and tactical terms of both games.

sections.title: San Antonio's case survives Puerto Rico's exit
paragraphs: San Antonio finished against China with 24 points, 9 rebounds, 7 assists and 5 steals. Her 5.0 steals per game remain the tournament standard. If Puerto Rico had reached overtime and advanced, one more high leverage defensive moment might have made her the clear favorite for Best Defensive Player.

With Puerto Rico out, Gabby Williams carries the strongest active case in the We Know the W Defensive Impact Rating at 96. Angel Reese follows at 92, with Rhyne Howard at 90. San Antonio's elimination changes the runway, not the quality of the résumé.

debates: Should team survival matter more than four games of elite defensive disruption?
Would Puerto Rico or Italy have controlled overtime after owning the late momentum?

posts.title: If We Knew Then What We Know Now: The 2024 WNBA Redraft
posts.dek: Two seasons of WNBA evidence changed the board. Caitlin Clark still goes first, Angel Reese jumps to No. 2, Sydney Taylor rockets from undrafted to No. 6, and the international guards force their way up the first round.

rows: Still the first call. Elite creation, range and playmaking keep the Fever right where they started.
The rebounding, production and night to night impact make her the clearest riser into the top tier.
Size, efficiency and two way value keep the 6 foot 7 center in the exact spot Chicago originally chose her.
A polished scoring forward with three level tools. The talent still looks worthy of the fourth pick.
Her growth as a creator pushes her four spots higher and gives Dallas a different answer at guard.
The class's biggest draft night reversal. An undrafted guard has played her way into the middle of Round 1.
Defensive pressure, pace and playmaking move the French guard into the top seven.
The ceiling is still enormous, but a redraft has to weigh availability and the WNBA sample we have actually seen.
Reliable frontcourt production keeps her safely in Round 1, even as several guards jump past her.
Still a first round guard, but the class has produced more high impact risers than draft night projected.
The second round pick earns a first round seat in the redo after proving she belongs in a WNBA rotation.
The upside and development case keep Atlanta's original final first round slot intact.

sections.title: The top stays Caitlin, but No. 2 changed everything
paragraphs: Caitlin Clark is the easy part of this exercise. Indiana had the first pick in 2024 and still makes the same call. The harder question starts immediately after her, because Angel Reese has erased the idea that seventh was the right place for her to wait.

Reese moves all the way to No. 2 in this redraft. Her rebounding has become a nightly game plan problem, her offensive responsibility has grown, and her impact is too large to leave outside the first two picks. That move alone reshapes the entire board.

sections.title: Cardoso and Jackson are the rare draft night holds
paragraphs: Kamilla Cardoso stays third and Rickea Jackson stays fourth. That is not a lack of movement, it is a compliment to how well those original selections have aged. Cardoso gives Chicago a massive interior presence with two way value. Jackson has shown the scoring package and positional versatility that made her one of the safest offensive prospects in the class.
In a redraft full of risers and slides, holding your original top four position is its own receipt.

sections.title: The middle of the round belongs to the risers
paragraphs: Carla Leite climbs from ninth to fifth, Sydney Taylor goes from undrafted to sixth, and Leila Lacan moves from tenth to seventh. That is the section of the board that looks most different with hindsight.

Leite and Lacan give this class two international guards whose WNBA translation looks stronger now than it did on draft night. Taylor is the loudest story of all. She was not one of the 36 names called in 2024. In this version, Washington takes her sixth. Draft night said undrafted. The floor said first round.

sections.title: Brink at eight is not a talent verdict
paragraphs: Cameron Brink dropping from second to eighth will be the pick people argue about most. The defensive ceiling is still obvious, and healthy Brink can change a game without needing touches. But a redraft based on what players have shown in the WNBA has to count availability and sample size alongside upside.
That makes eighth a statement about the evidence available today, not a claim that seven players have a higher long term ceiling.

sections.title: Round 1 has two new names
paragraphs: Aaliyah Edwards and Jacy Sheldon remain in the first round, but both slide as the risers pass them. Isobel Borlase makes one of the quieter jumps, moving from pick 20 into the No. 11 slot. Nyadiew Puoch stays at 12, preserving Atlanta's original selection.

The two original first rounders who fall out are Alissa Pili, originally eighth, and Marquesha Davis, originally eleventh. That does not erase what got them drafted. It shows how quickly a class can reorder itself once projection turns into professional evidence.

sections.title: Shak's takeaway: draft night is the opening sentence
paragraphs: The fun of a redraft is not pretending front offices should have known the future. It is seeing which skills translated, which opportunities changed careers, and which players forced the league to reconsider the label attached to them.

The 2024 class now has a No. 1 who still looks like No. 1, a No. 7 who looks like No. 2, and an undrafted player who looks like a lottery level selection. That is why the draft matters, but development, health, fit and opportunity get the last word.

sections.title: One important note about the team logos
paragraphs: The teams on this redraft board follow the original 2024 first round draft order. They are not the players' current teams. The question is simple: if each franchise could make its 2024 selection again with what we know now, who would it take?

debates: Does Angel Reese have the strongest case for the biggest rise in the 2024 class?
How high would a fully healthy Cameron Brink go if the redraft were based on ceiling instead of WNBA evidence to date?
Is Sydney Taylor the best undrafted success story from this class?
Which international guard would you take first today, Carla Leite or Leila Lacan?

foodSegment.title: Draft Night Is a Receipt, Not a Life Sentence
foodSegment.script: Caitlin still goes one. Angel refuses to wait until seven. Carla and Leila move up the line, and Sydney Taylor walks into the first round without ever hearing her name called on draft night. That is the whole point of the redo. Scouts draft projections. The league grades translation. Two years later, this class has handed us a very different receipt.

posts.title: Four Months, Four Receipts: Is the Rookie of the Year Race Already Olivia Miles’ ?
posts.dek: Olivia Miles has won every Kia Rookie of the Month award available this season. That makes her the clear leader, but Flau'jae Johnson, Sydney Taylor, Azzi Fudd and Kiki Rice still tell us something important about how deep this rookie class really is.

rows: 19.7 PPG, 4.6 RPG, 6.0 APG through 38 games, plus all four Kia Rookie of the Month awards.
14.1 PPG, 4.8 RPG, 2.9 APG with two way impact, plus the No. 1 W Score on the latest We Know the W Rookie of the Week board.
14.7 PPG as an undrafted rookie, one of the best pure scoring stories in the class.
13.1 PPG and 1.7 steals per game before a right knee procedure ended her rookie season.
11.2 PPG, 4.0 RPG and 2.8 APG while carrying real creation responsibility for an expansion team.

sections.title: Four months is a pattern, not a hot streak
paragraphs: There is a point in every award race when we have to stop asking who is ahead and start asking what someone else would have to do to catch them. Olivia Miles has reached that point. May belonged to Miles. June belonged to Miles. July belonged to Miles. August belonged to Miles. Four months in the league, four Kia Rookie of the Month awards.

The August receipt might be the loudest one yet. Miles averaged 20.6 points, 4.3 rebounds and 6.5 assists for the month. That is not rookie production being graded on a curve. That is lead guard production on a team trying to win the whole thing.

sections.title: The strongest challenger is making the weekly argument
paragraphs: Flau'jae Johnson has not matched Miles month for month, but she keeps building the kind of case that survives beyond one statistic. She scores, rebounds, defends and has taken on important possessions for Seattle without looking like the moment is too big.

The latest We Know the W Rookie of the Week board is a perfect example. Johnson finished Week 14 at No. 1 with a 29.1 W Score after averaging 19.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.0 assists across two games. A weekly board does not decide Rookie of the Year, but it shows who is applying pressure right now.

sections.title: Sydney Taylor is the reminder that draft night is not destiny
paragraphs: Sydney Taylor was not drafted. She also entered September averaging 14.7 points per game. Those two sentences belong next to each other because they explain why this rookie class deserves more attention than one trophy race can hold.

Taylor's Rookie of the Year path is harder because Miles has the stronger all around case and a full season of monthly hardware, but Taylor has already turned an undrafted label into a footnote. That is a different kind of rookie victory.

sections.title: Azzi Fudd's season ended, her impact did not
paragraphs: The No. 1 pick was still firmly in the rookie conversation before right knee soreness led to a season ending arthroscopic procedure. Fudd finished her year at 13.1 points, 1.7 rebounds, 1.8 assists and 1.7 steals per game, while shooting 39.7 percent from three.

Availability matters in an award race, especially against a player producing at Miles' level across a longer season. Still, Fudd's rookie year gave Dallas shooting, point of attack defense and a historic All Star weekend moment when she became the first rookie to win the WNBA three point contest.

sections.title: Kiki Rice has the expansion tax
paragraphs: Kiki Rice's numbers do not jump off the page the way Miles' do, but context matters. Toronto is building a team and an identity at the same time, and Rice has been asked to create inside that uncertainty. An 11 point scoring average with rebounding and playmaking responsibility is a strong foundation for a first year guard.

The Rookie of the Year ballot is not a projection award, so upside alone cannot move Rice ahead of Miles today. But if we are asking which rookies look like long term franchise pieces, Rice belongs in the conversation.

sections.title: So, is there still a race?
paragraphs: Technically, yes. Basketball still has games left, and awards should not be handed out before the schedule is finished. Practically, Olivia Miles has built a gap that now requires an extraordinary closing argument from everyone behind her and a real decline from Miles herself.

The better question might be what kind of Rookie of the Year season we are watching. Miles is not simply leading rookies in a weak class. She is putting up nearly 20 points and six assists a night for Minnesota while sweeping the league's monthly rookie awards. That makes this less about whether she belongs at the top and more about how high her rookie season will eventually sit in WNBA history.

sections.title: What I am watching next
paragraphs: The weekly archive matters now because it can show us whether the gap is tightening before a season average catches up. If Johnson keeps stacking No. 1 weekly W Scores, if Taylor keeps scoring at this level and if Rice closes with a bigger creation load, the race gets more interesting even if the favorite does not change.
For now, the ballot starts with Olivia Miles. The rest of the rookie class is not disappearing behind her. It is giving us several different versions of what a successful first season can look like.

posts.title: So, About That Lynx Blueprint... Atlanta Added a Chapter
posts.dek: Golden State showed the pressure version. Atlanta showed the possession version. With Courtney Williams back and Minnesota still losing, the Lynx blueprint is getting harder to dismiss.

sections.title: Atlanta added a second chapter
paragraphs: The Dream beat Minnesota 89 to 81 with Courtney Williams back in the Lynx lineup, shrinking the biggest asterisk attached to the earlier Golden State loss.
Atlanta did not copy Golden State. The Dream won the glass, hit 13 threes, moved the ball through multiple creators and showed there is more than one way to make Minnesota uncomfortable.

posts.title: Standings Show the Record. Power Rankings Show the Temperature.
posts.dek: Minnesota owns the official table, but Golden State owns the latest We Know the W power ranking. Here is where momentum changes the order.

sections.title: The table and the temperature
paragraphs: Golden State rises to No. 1 after a four win week, while official leader Minnesota drops to fourth following consecutive losses to Golden State and Atlanta.
Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles and Seattle each rank two places higher than their official standing. Las Vegas, Indiana, Washington and Connecticut land in exactly the same position on both lists.

sources.label: We Know the W August 31 power-ranking edition

posts.title: The Dream Beat the Lynx. Now Minnesota Has a Pattern Problem.
posts.dek: Atlanta beat Minnesota 89 to 81, won the season series 2 to 1 and handed the Lynx a second straight loss. The methods were different from Golden State, but the pressure points are starting to look repeatable.

sections.title: A different version of the blueprint
paragraphs: Atlanta did not need to win the turnover battle. The Dream made 13 threes to Minnesota's six, outrebounded the Lynx 37 to 32 and built a 52 to 41 halftime lead.

Allisha Gray finished with 23 points and 11 rebounds, Jordin Canada had 16 points and 10 assists, and Angel Reese recorded 15 points and 11 rebounds for a WNBA record 29th double double of the season. Olivia Miles scored 21 for Minnesota but finished with zero assists.

posts.title: Kelsey Mitchell Is the WNBA's First 1,000 Point Guard
posts.dek: Mitchell's 34 against Connecticut pushed her to 1,001 points, making her the first guard and only the second player ever to score 1,000 in one WNBA season.

sections.title: The line moved
paragraphs: A'ja Wilson created the 1,000 point season club. Kelsey Mitchell just became its first guard, reaching the mark with elite efficiency and a season that is still moving.

posts.title: A’ja Wilson's Name Is Written Into South Carolina's Nike Deal

sections.title: Boardroom leverage, with receipts
paragraphs: The public record does not prove Wilson singlehandedly caused the Nike deal. It does show something unusually concrete: her signature product and marketing connection carry explicit contractual value inside a university wide agreement covering all 21 Gamecocks programs.
